## **About 12126 PRAGATI EXPRESS**

## 12126 PRAGATI EXPRESS: Train Route, Schedule and Timings

PRAGATI EXPRESS runs between Pune Junction and C Shivaji Mah T Railway Station. Regarding PRAGATI EXPRESS timings, this train departs at 07:45 AM from the source station to arrive at the destination station at 11:25 AM . Total duration of the train from Pune Junction to C Shivaji Mah T Railway Station is 3 hrs 40 mins . PRAGATI EXPRESS runs from Pune Junction on 7 days a week ( Friday, Monday, Saturday, Sunday, Thursday, Tuesday, Wednesday ). There are 7 stoppages between Pune Junction and C Shivaji Mah T Railway Station .

PRAGATI EXPRESS route covers [Lonavala(LNL)](https://www.goibibo.com/trains/lonavala-railway-station-lnl-stn/), [Karjat(KJT)](https://www.goibibo.com/trains/karjat-railway-station-kjt-stn/), [Panvel(PNVL)](https://www.goibibo.com/trains/panvel-railway-station-pnvl-stn/), [Thane(TNA)](https://www.goibibo.com/trains/thane-railway-station-tna-stn/), [Dadar Central(DR)](https://www.goibibo.com/trains/mumbai-dadar-central-railway-station-dr-stn/). Finally, it arrives at C Shivaji Mah T Railway Station. It covers the distance of 118 KM km in 3 hrs 40 mins .

### About Pune

Nestled in the heart of Maharashtra, Pune is a city that beautifully blends the old with the new. Known for its rich cultural heritage and modern lifestyle, Pune is often referred to as the 'Queen of the Deccan'. The city is a bustling hub of academia, with numerous prestigious universities and colleges earning it the moniker 'Oxford of the East'. Pune's vibrant culture, historical significance, and scenic beauty make it a must-visit destination for travelers.

Whether you're exploring its ancient forts, attending a classical music concert, or indulging in local delicacies, Pune offers a unique experience that caters to all kinds of travelers. The city's historical landmarks, such as the Shaniwar Wada and Aga Khan Palace, tell tales of its glorious past, while its modern infrastructure and lively nightlife reflect its contemporary spirit. Pune is also known for its spiritual centers, including the Osho International Meditation Resort, which attracts visitors from around the world seeking peace and tranquility.

**Best Time to Visit**

Pune enjoys a moderate climate throughout the year, making it a pleasant destination to visit any time. However, the best time to explore Pune is from July to March. During these months, the weather is cool and comfortable, ideal for sightseeing and outdoor activities. The monsoon season, from July to September, brings lush greenery and a refreshing atmosphere, perfect for nature lovers. The winter months, from October to March, are particularly enjoyable with mild temperatures and clear skies, making it the peak tourist season.

Summers in Pune, from April to June, can be hot and dry, but the evenings are usually pleasant. If you prefer fewer crowds and lower accommodation rates, visiting during the off-peak summer season might be a good option.

**Places to Explore in Pune**

Pune is a treasure trove of attractions that cater to diverse interests. History enthusiasts can explore the majestic Shaniwar Wada, a historic fortification that offers a glimpse into the Maratha Empire. The Aga Khan Palace, another significant landmark, is not only an architectural marvel but also a site of historical importance where Mahatma Gandhi was imprisoned.

For adventure seekers, Sinhagad Fort provides thrilling trekking trails and panoramic views of the surrounding landscape. Religious sites such as the Dagadusheth Halwai Ganapati Temple, Pataleshwar Cave Temple, and Chaturshringi Temple offer spiritual solace and architectural beauty. The National War Museum is a must-visit for those interested in India's military history.

Don't miss the Osho International Meditation Resort, a serene haven for those looking to rejuvenate their mind and body. Pune's vibrant markets, such as Laxmi Road and Fergusson College Road, are perfect for shopping and experiencing the local culture.

**Airport Details**

Pathetic hotel. Stayed here for 1 night with family in January 2017. Over the counter booking. Rs. 1800 for 2 non-ac double rooms. 1 room was very very small. Rooms & washrooms were not so clean. There was lots of dust on sides of bed & below the mattress. Service was worst. The hotel has a restaurant at 1st floor. It was already late & the restaurant was suppose to close so we decided to have dinner in our rooms but the owner told us that we have to pay 15% extra for serving the food in room. It was a surprise for us. I stayed in hundreds of hotels in different cities but no hotel has this type of condition. His justification was that if you have dinner in rooms than there will be some spilling etc hence to clean & maintain that they charge 15% extra. I was in total shock. So to save 15% I told them to pack the food as parcel & just give us plates & spoons but to that also they refused & instructed the room boys not to provide anything. All hotels provide plates, glasses & spoons to their guests on request. It is an amenity. Even non-restaurant hotels provide these things on request. On too much request the room boy provided only spoons but they were dirty & not washed at all. Finally we used the paper plates which we had with us & had the food with our hands. The food was not even packed in containers but in polythene covers. My first pathetic experience like this.

Even for this kind of hotel the owner was praising about his hotel like there is no hotel in whole India like this. He told me that at this rate you cannot find any hotel in India as good as his hotel. I don't have any words to tell him at that time.

Just 1 day back we stayed at Hotel Sai Bansi in Shirdi & just for Rs. 900 (got good offer with MMT) for 2 ac rooms. Beautiful property, clean rooms, prompt service, good restaurant with all amenities. In fact it was also late night check-in so on our request they kept our food packed at the reception & provided us plates, spoons, glasses etc in the rooms with just 1 call. This is called professional hotel management.

Stayed at Hotel Radhika Palace, Parbhani as we didn't had any other choice at that time otherwise cannot stay at place like this.

My humble request to owner to check other cities's hotels & improve please. Be professional.

I've travelled a lot, and this place has to be the worst place we ever stayed in. We booked an AC room. We checked in at 9 pm, so the booking should have run until 9 pm the following day, since this is the hotel policy.

These were the issues we had. In the more expensive AC room:

1\. The floor wasn't swept

2\. There was a thick layer of dust on the side tables etc

3\. The bathroom was filthy - with a layer of sticky gunk on the sink and toilet. It is obvious this hadn't been washed.

4\. I gagged on the smell of the bedsheets - obvious it hadn't been washed

5\. Towels and sheets were stained

We had two children with us, so we asked for two extra mattresses, which we paid extra for. The staff put the mattresses on the floor, put bedsheets, then WALKED OVER the newly-made bed, leaving filthy shoe stains. They did not bother to replace the bedsheets, and they did not apologize.

We had a wedding to go to the following morning, and my husband wasn't sure if we'd stay at the wedding or come back for the afternoon, so my husband left the luggage at the reception with clear instructions to not give our room away (since it was paid for till 9:00 p.m.).

We come back, and sure enough, the AC room is given away. The hotel manager couldn't deny that we still had a reservation, so he offered to put us up in a non-AC room. It was very very hot, so we asked if there were AC rooms available. The manager said all the rooms were taken. When the assistant said the AC suite was still available - the manager blatantly cut him off, telling us a long, involved story about how this suite was reserved just that very morning.

So we were shoved into a really small non-AC bedroom with no extra child mattresses that we had already paid for. It was brutally hot, the room had absolutely no air circulation.

You'd be better off sleeping on the footpath.

The chaotic streets jammed with rickshaws, meandering goats munching piles of trash, & the visible clash of ancient tradition with industrial innovation, all make it one of the most interesting cities in India. A city with just as many skyscrapers as Hindi temples, Mumbai is a city of contradictions. After all, it’s the home of Bollywood, the most expensive house in the entire world, & India’s business elite, but it’s also the home of _[Dharavi](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=47&marker=295548&p=1922&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.viator.com%2Ftours%2FMumbai%2FPrivate-Walking-Tour-of-Dharavi-Slum%2Fd953-34181P5%3Fapi_version%3D2.0&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=qGcvfviP6tcTgkdZ8vXkB&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F)_– Asia’s largest slum, and a vast world of street food.

**& Mumbai is packed with free things to do in the city.**

Mumbai is also immense. It is so large it could be a country in itself. 20.1 million people and counting. The city even contains a national park complete with prowling wild leopards. I can see why so many travelers find it overwhelming & have a difficult time separating the worthwhile attractions from the waste of time. I’ll break it down for you.

**Let’s start with some tidbits you should know about Mumbai before you dive right in.**

### **Haggling is key.**

Prices in India are not set in stone. Haggling is part of the culture here and you should expect to bargain with all vendors aside from those selling food.

### **You will get attention as a foreigner.**

There’s just no way around it. I was surprised that in a city where spotting foreigners seemed commonplace, locals seemed eager to snap a quick photo. If you don’t want to take photos with crowds of locals like a Hollywood celebrity, don’t be afraid to give a firm no.

### **Be prepared with small bills.**

In any other country, I would discourage giving money to child beggars but in Mumbai (& the rest of India) it’s a tricky situation. The ethics are ambiguous, but after being followed across 7 train stations by a sobbing child, I learned it’s often just easier to hand over a few coins. The locals do it too. Small change is also handy for street vendors and performers that you’ll encounter throughout the day.

### **Start small and work toward longer days**

Mumbai is huge, and sensory overload is practically guaranteed. It helps to break the city into bite-sized pieces and start with the easier to swallow ones, like Southern Mumbai. It’s the most tourist-friendly area and will cause the least amount of culture shock fresh off the plane.

### **Mumbai is more about the experience & less about checking off a bucketlist.**

Don’t get me wrong, there is plenty to see in Mumbai but it’s not really a “tourist-friendly” city. Attractions are spread out and often just seeing the city in action is far more impressive. Just learn to embrace the chaos.

## **15 Free (or Almost Free) Things to do in Mumbai**

### 1\. **Eat Your Heart Out**

Compare every modern metropolis that travelers fall in love with & they all seem to have one thing in common…a killer food scene. & Mumbai is no different.

![](https://beyondthebucketlist.co/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/IMG_5231-768x1024.jpeg)A typical Indian Breakfast![](https://beyondthebucketlist.co/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/IMG_5200-768x1024.jpeg)One of my most favorite dishes in India![](https://beyondthebucketlist.co/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/IMG_5452-768x1024.jpeg)Chaat. A typical Indian snack food

The mish-mash of cultures and cuisines that create good food is always at its best in a big city. Here in Mumbai, you have your traditional Northern & Southern Indian styles meshing to become something all its own. Pakistani & Iranian cuisines have a stronghold in Mumbai as well, but really, you can find almost any type of cuisine done remarkably well in Mumbai.

So eat. From the $0.25 street food bites to the local lunch spots to the Michelin starred meals, Mumbai undoubtedly has some of the best bites in India, and you should sample it all.

**Keep in mind India is a vegetarian paradise**. So much, in fact, restaurants advertise “non-vegetarian” if they serve meat, otherwise assume veggie is the standard. I promise you won’t even miss the meat.

### **2\. Spend a Day in Dharavi**

Asia’s largest slum. [Dharavi](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=108&marker=295548&p=3965&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.getyourguide.com%2Fmumbai-l201%2Fmumbai-slum-tour-visit-dharavi-slum-with-local-guide-t626489%2F%3Fcurrency%3DUSD%26psrc%3Dpartner_api&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=SeNM9q75WTQf359hwONR2&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F) is home to more than 1 million people, all crammed into an area smaller than [central park](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=47&marker=295548&p=1922&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.viator.com%2Fx-attractions%2Fy%2Fd0-a1283%3Fapi_version%3D2.0&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=7boXVOyBKzenTfAKEx3tx&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F). & you just might recognize it from the movie Slumdog Millionaire. Self-built houses stack one on top of another in a maze of corrugated metal and 2 ft. wide walkways. With none of it officially built or inspected, it’s a bit of an invisible city within a city. But against all odds, it thrives. Every street is lined with food, markets, open-air leather making, and pottery shops. As well as being one of the most interesting neighborhoods in Mumbai to wander, it’s also one of the best for street art.

![Free things to do in Mumbai. Slums of dharavi ](<Base64-Image-Removed>)Just outside the slums of Dharavi. This is the train station at Mahim.

**How to visit with a group**: One of the most popular (and controversial) tourist attractions in Mumbai is to take a “slum tour”. But visiting doesn’t have to be poverty porn. Some organizations are respectful and informative giving 95% of the profits to community development and the schools in Dharavi. Another good indicator of a respectful organization is if the group discourages bringing your camera. Just be sure to research the group before you sign up.

**Want to visit on your own?** Personally, I think visiting Dharavi independently is the best way to interact with the locals, give back to the community, & get a look at what life in [Dharavi](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=84&marker=295548&p=2076&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.booking.com%2Fsearchresults.en-gb.html%3Fdest_id%3D900055209%26dest_type%3Dlandmark&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=MkxqDu7gjgqm8-qazyKpX&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F) is like. Without the filtered lens of an organized tour.

#### **Tips for visiting Dharavi Independently**

- Take the train to _Mahim_ station and then begin your tour on foot. A visit via rickshaw will not suffice.
- Get lost and wander down every narrow alleyway. The street art is mostly on the perimeter of the town but all the action happens deep inside.
- Talk to locals and buy local goods! It’s a great way to support the economy.
- Don’t be nervous! If you visit on your own accord just don’t bring a large camera or snap photos of people without permission. Be respectful and friendly and you’ll be met with smiling faces.

### **3\. Buy Back Your Stuff at Chor Bazaar or the Thieves Market**

As the story goes, if you ever lose something in Mumbai you’ll likely find it here– at the Thieves Market. Specializing in antiques and home goods, you’ll also find entire cars stripped piece by piece, and tucked into the center is a huge indoor wet market. You can easily spend an entire afternoon wandering the coiling streets just “window” shopping.

![](<Base64-Image-Removed>)![](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

#### **& while you’re at it browse some of Mumbai’s other impressive markets**.

- **Bhuleshwar Bazaar** is a massive wholesale market known for its cheap jewelry in Southern Mumbai.
- **Linking Road Market**. Take a peek at the residential alleyways of [Bandra](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=84&marker=295548&p=2076&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.booking.com%2Fsearchresults.en-gb.html%3Fdest_id%3D3445%26dest_type%3Ddistrict&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=FjN36jrgWmYfrCZK1Q1nA&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F) where clothing shops slowly turn into fruits and vegetable stands.

### **4\. Marvel at Dobi Ghat**

![open air laundry. Tall buildings in Mumbai. ](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

Step off the _Mahalaxmi_ train platform and take in all of Mumbai’s laundry hung out to dry. [Dobi Ghat](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=108&marker=295548&p=3965&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.getyourguide.com%2Fmumbai-l201%2Fmumbai-best-dhobi-ghat-laundry-dharavi-slum-tour-by-a-local-t597182%2F%3Fcurrency%3DUSD%26psrc%3Dpartner_api&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=cQ6VjLfIUsqRCxG8GTrPR&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F) is an outdoor laundry run entirely by men. From this vantage point, you’ll see rows upon rows of color-coded uniforms from all Mumbai’s hospitals and hotels. Beneath the spider-web of clotheslines are the Dhobis themselves, diligently stomping dirty clothes into the washing pits and then wringing out the murky water garment by garment. The entire process is played out beneath you and you might be thinking…why would I want to watch someone do laundry? But just trust me, it’s worth a look.

### **5\. See the Most Elaborately Designed Train Station**

![Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus train station in mumbai ](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus is both a mouthful and an eyeful. Whoever designed this train station must have thought it was going to be used by royalty. You have to go across the street to see it in all its glory. It’s a Gothic Victorian design that’s all spires and dramatic archways. & a fully functional railway station to boot.

### **6\. Take a Walk Past the Oval Maiden**

Here you can see two of the national pass times in action. Cricket & fútbol. Universally loved and religiously followed, cricket and fútbol are as much a part of Mumbai culture as Ganesh and Naan.

### **7\. Be a Spectacle at the Gateway of India**

![gateway of india. Things to do in Mumbai. ](https://beyondthebucketlist.co/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/DSC_1230-1024x683.jpg)

The jewel of Southern Mumbai. The elaborately designed archway sitting on the Arabian sea is worth a visit just to snap a few photos. Since it’s the top tourist destination in Mumbai for Indian nationals as well as travelers, it’s a madhouse of activity. & weirdly enough a lot of attention will be focused on you. Locals love to take photos with foreigners and if you happen to have red-hair or some other exciting physical attribute the attention will be even more pronounced.

### **8\. Visit the Temples on Elephanta Island**

From the moment you arrive at the gateway of India, you’ll be bombarded by local touts selling tickets to the cave temples just 10km offshore. As off-putting as the eager salesman can be, the UNESCO-World Heritage site crafted in 5-8 CE and dedicated to the god Shiva, is a really impressive cave temple complex.

### **9\. Join the Evening Prayer at the Haji Ali Dargah**

![Haji Mosque. Things to do for free in Mumbai. ](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

There are loads of holy sites worthy of your time in Mumbai, but none are as interesting as the Haji Ali Dargah. Sitting off the West coast of Mumbai, like a buoy floating in the sea, the mosque is only accessible at low tide when a small pathway becomes exposed. Join the throngs of pilgrims on Thursdays and Fridays that flock to the mosque to pay their respects. Just be sure to bring a headscarf if you are a woman.

**[Bandra](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=84&marker=295548&p=2076&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.booking.com%2Fsearchresults.en-gb.html%3Fdest_id%3D3445%26dest_type%3Ddistrict&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=3IfZzpp4biWebz-QBnLRD&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F)** tops the list as one of my favorite Mumbai neighborhoods. ### **13\. Witness the Magic of the Bandra-Worli Sea Link**

[Bandra-Worli Sea Link](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=84&marker=295548&p=2076&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.booking.com%2Fsearchresults.en-gb.html%3Fdest_id%3D900055057%26dest_type%3Dlandmark&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=tu-qqQrkebbsqgA1XDRPJ&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F) is a modern architectural marvel. Perch up at the sea-link viewpoint in the evening to watch the 6 km long futuristic bridge glow with the taillights of traffic while the waves lap at its concrete feet.

### **14\. Spot Leopards at Sanjay Gandhi National Park**

Mumbai is so massive that it has an entire 34 square mile national park sitting inside it. This sprawling green-space even has 35 resident leopards in its midst, as well as the Kanheri caves dated to 1 BCE. Only the luckiest travelers will spot the prowling predators but everyone can enjoy the hikes and viewpoints within the park.

**Travel Tip**: The caves are closed on Mondays and the park charges an entrance fee of 58 Rupees per person.

### **15\. Visit a local fishing market**

Mumbai’s original inhabitants were fishermen. The city’s roots are in the sea. And there are plenty of local fish markets that pay homage to that history. If you’ve visited the [beaches of Sri Lanka](https://beyondthebucketlist.co/sri-lankas-best-beaches-which-one-is-right-for-you/), you’ll probably have seen these fishy outdoor markets before.

- **[Worli Fishing Village](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=47&marker=295548&p=1922&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.viator.com%2Ftours%2FMumbai%2FWorli-Fishing-Village-Tour%2Fd953-10591P37%3Fapi_version%3D2.0&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=6Zu_2XvE3dQG1TMUT4a1c&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F)**. Walking through this colorful little fishing town is like stepping back in history.
- **[Sassoon Docks Fish Market](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=47&marker=295548&p=1922&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.viator.com%2Ftours%2FMumbai%2FKarla-and-Bhaja-Caves-Tour%2Fd953-139993P11%3Fapi_version%3D2.0&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=VzhOyW6jdmyNjJjKuFM9Z&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F)**. One of the oldest and craziest fish markets in Mumbai. Visit before 6:30 AM to see the Koli fisherman and women at work.
- **[Crawford Market](https://emrldtp.com/re?campaign_id=84&marker=295548&p=2076&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.booking.com%2Fsearchresults.en-gb.html%3Fdest_id%3D261340%26dest_type%3Dlandmark&trs=36136&trace_id=Zz8f81c25c7b6c4861b3747b0-295548&install_type=am_partner_content&product_type=emerald&journey_id=vo2x82i-t_GLc0fykBFXc&promo_kind=tp_other&page_url=https%3A%2F%2Fbeyondthebucketlist.co%2F15-free-things-to-do-in-mumbai%2F).** The early bird gets the best fish. Make sure to get here at 6-7 AM to see the fish auctions in all their glory.

## Bonus Activity: Celebrate Holi in March

If your visit to India coincides with the Hindu celebration of Spring you are in for a technicolored treat.

A near country-wide water & neon paint fight that’s contagiously fun. You can take to the streets and smear strangers with pastel powder or you can join in a small organized event often held at hostels and bars or one of the massive Holi festival parties complete with world-famous DJs and unlimited Bhang Lassi. _Bhang Lassi is an intoxicating yogurt beverage infused with THC or Marijuana._ & it packs a punch so indulge lightly. The date changes every year so be sure to check before you book your trip.

![woman covered in holi paint. Free things to do in Mumbai. ](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

Mumbai is unlike any other city in the country. & with this itinerary, you’ll be able to capture the city in all its diverse glory. From its seaman roots to the heavy colonial influence still plainly visible today, you’ll get a little bit of everything. **You can spend as little as $20 per day on a bare-bones budget trip to the city.** So if you’re looking for amazing food, architectural wonders, and a city as authentically Indian as it gets, you’re in the right place.

### Mumbai’s Best Street Food Tour!

## [Mumbai’s Best Street Food Tour!](https://mumbaidreamtours.com/mumbais-best-street-food-tour/)

- August 19, 2019December 2, 2025

**What better way to sample some of this food that we have been so curious about, foods we have been seeing as we toured the city on our own.  It was great to have a guide, to explain to us what we were eating and what was (hopefully!) safe to eat. I did have some concerns that we could be paying for this little adventure over the next few days, but Sagar, our guide, assured us that everything we were about to eat was clean safe [food](https://mumbaidreamtours.com/portfolio/street-food-tour/).**

**The tour started at Chowpatty, Mumbai’s beach and local hang out spot.  There were many stands here selling food, most of them looked to be selling the same foods.  Its kind of reminded me of buying food at a carnival.  This was a Hindu area of town and everything that we would be eating here would be vegetarian.**

![](https://i0.wp.com/mumbaidreamtours.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Gol-Gappa-Panipuri-Indian-Spicy-Food-HD-Wallpaper-06047-300x225.jpg?resize=300%2C225)

#### _**Pani Puri**_

**The first thing we tried was pani puri.  A hollow ball of crusty dough, almost like a taco chip, was punctured by the thumb of the man serving the food and filled with a cold water mixture of what looked like corn and something green.**

**I could count five things in the preparation of this food with the potential to get us ill…should we really be doing this?**

**The four of us were served our pani puri.  The proper way to eat it was to put the entire thing into your mouth and eat it.  It is quite a large bite of food!  I bit into mine, sending a surprising explosion of cold, spicy, vegetable water into my mouth.  I can’t say that I really liked it.  Still, I went back for seconds, but that was enough for me.**

![](https://i0.wp.com/mumbaidreamtours.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Chaat-Featured-300x158.jpg?resize=300%2C158)

#### _**Dahi Batata Puri**_

**Next up was Dahi batata puri. After stuffing the puri and topping it with sauces and copious amounts of creamy Dahi, he hands us the plate with a flourish and we proceed to dig in. This was awesome.  Those same puri shells were filled with some vegetable mixture, hot this time, and not watery, then doused with yogurt and herbs.  So, so good!**

![](https://i0.wp.com/mumbaidreamtours.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Pav-Bhaji-300x237.jpg?resize=300%2C237)

#### _**Pav Bhaji**_

**The third dish we tried turned out to be a family favorite, pav bhaji.  This part of India was first settled by the Portuguese, and this dish has a Portuguese origin.  Tomatoes and other vegetables are cooked and mashed together and Indian spices are added to it.  We ate the bread with the vegetable mixture and it was awesome.  I could eat this every day.**

![](https://i0.wp.com/mumbaidreamtours.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/IMG_2186-300x200.jpg?resize=300%2C200)

#### _**Kulfi**_

**Next up, another family favorite and something sweet this time.  Kulfi is sweetened condensed milk with added flavorings, then frozen. Any flavors can be added, however, the assortment of Kulfi flavors we enjoyed were pistachio, mango, vanilla, rosewater, cardamom and cashew nut – all traditional delicious Indian flavors.  This was perfect on a hot night and it was so good that we went back for seconds.**

![](https://i0.wp.com/mumbaidreamtours.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/chicken-tikka-roll-on-mumbai-street-food-guide-300x180.jpg?resize=300%2C180)

#### _**Chicken Rolls and Sandwiches**_

**Part one of the tour was over.  To get to the next location, a predominantly Muslim neighborhood in Mumbai, we had to take a twenty-minute taxi ride across town.  Now it was time for some meat dishes.**

**We took our seats in the back of a very small restaurant.  It was very warm in the back, even at 8 pm.  Here we ate chicken rolls, a dish made of beef and eggs in a flat pastry, and a spicy chicken sandwich.  It was all very good, especially the spicy chicken sandwich.**

![](https://i0.wp.com/mumbaidreamtours.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/sancha-ice-cream-7-bungalows-versova-andheri-mumbai-callmehi5-300x223.jpg?resize=300%2C223)

#### _**Ice Cream**_

**Ice cream time!  There’s always room for ice cream, especially homemade ice cream. Everything that needs to be said about Taj Icecream has probably been said. The outlet is over 125 years old, and if it isn’t the oldest ice cream place in the city, we don’t know what is. Its charm exists in the traditional preparation of ice cream, still churned by hand. That the place isn’t ideal to hang out at is a small mercy, or we’d be there for dessert all night. Everything tastes good here, and it’s arguably the best traditional ice creams in the city. we were the biggest fans of this dish.**

**Our food tour ended at Taj Icecream.  What a wonderful experience.  I love trying new foods, especially strange new foods.  And I am very happy to say that none of us got sick after this tour, a very wonderful thing since we had a plane to catch to Udaipur the next day.**

**This feeling of discovery continues long after such tours end, especially when food becomes intertwined with atmosphere, creativity and shared experiences beyond the plate. There is something uplifting about places where meals are paired with community, and the way conversations, music and good food can blend into a single warm memory. [Khaleejesque local musicians & great food post](https://khaleejesque.me/2017/02/06/melenzane-presents-local-musicians-and-great-food/ "") captures this spirit beautifully, showing how the energy around a meal can be just as nourishing as the food itself.**

**The idea that a dining experience can be elevated by the people around you mirrors the joy we felt on the tour, where the unfamiliar became welcoming and the simple act of tasting something new became a celebration. It is this blend of flavor, story and shared enthusiasm that makes food adventures so unforgettable, whether on a bustling street or in a cozy venue filled with music.**

**So, if anyone has plans to tour Mumbai, put the street food tour with** [**Mumbai Dream Tours**](https://www.mumbaidreamtours.com/) **at the top of your life.**

A variety of affordable hotels, including The Caliph are situated near scenic lakes and Sanjay Gandhi National Park. Alternatively, for families who don’t mind the hustle and bustle, Andheri East is a lively district with mid-range hotels and close access to the Metro. - ### Are there good hotels near Mumbai airport? #### The hotels closest to Mumbai’s large, sprawling airport (known as Chhatrapati Shivaji International) are situated just opposite the arrivals terminal. Highly-rated options like The Orchid and Sahara Star can be found here. North of the building, along Sahar Airport Road, you’ll also find a crop of international chains, including the Hilton and Hyatt Regency. - ### Which neighbourhoods are close to Mumbai’s central train station? #### The area around Mumbai’s central train station is known quite simply as Mumbai Central. It’s where you’ll find smart business hotels like the 3-star Sahil Hotel, with its tastefully-decorated rooms and chic restaurant. Other neighbourhoods to stay in include Tardeo and Malabar Hill west of the station, and Dongri and Pydhonie to the east. - ### Where are the best hotels near the Gateway of India? #### High-class hotels abound in the affluent neighbourhood of Colaba, where the iconic Gateway of India is located. Last Updated on October 25, 2024 by [Ellen](https://www.earthvagabonds.com/)

If you’re going to splurge on anything in Mumbai, India, during your visit, I’d recommend you spend the extra money on your accommodations. There are enough fun **free things to do in Mumbai**, so you don’t have to spend a lot on excursions – if you don’t want to.

To this American, Mumbai felt like an Indian cross between Los Angeles and New York. Of course, general prices are much lower than in the USA, but even us budget slow travelers found out rentals (and real estate in general) is at a premium in this mega city. The most basic Airbnbs in this Indian city cost more than in bigger cities of other Asian countries like Thailand or the Philippines.

You can eat cheap, or not. There are plenty of options at every price level. You can also find cultural events and museums and pay entry fees.

But again I say: spend your extra money on accommodations. After wandering around the city streets in a mega city, you will enjoy a return to a clean, quiet, comfy home base.

### Getting around to the fun stuff

An ideally located ‘home base’ in the Colaba area will help in your quest to experience free things to do in Mumbai. Actually, any neighborhood near common bus routes and train tracks can save money on getting around.

Uber and Ola are readily available, as are a million taxis, but those e-hail car rides will cost you two bucks or more to go a couple of kilometers.

Trains and buses – if you have the patience – cost around 10 to 25 cents depending on your destination. (I don’t recommend travel on public transport during rush hours – it is crazy crowded.)

Rickshaws, aka tuktuks, are not available in the city center, but dominate the roads in places like Juhu and Bandra. Base fare starts at 21 rupees. We always rounded up for a little tip – at which the drivers were delighted.

![train in mumbai](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20800%20600'%3E%3C/svg%3E)![rickshaw in bandra section of mumbai](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20800%20600'%3E%3C/svg%3E)![rickshaw traffic in mumbai](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20900%20401'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Mumbai has the cheapest tuktuks in India, because, as you can see above, the competition is fierce — and so they all uses meters! A 20 minute ride will cost literally a few cents. This is unlike places like Puducherry – where Caucasians are frequently gauged and meters are unheard of.

## Top 10 free things to do in Mumbai

### 1\. Hall of Culture at the Nehru Centre

- Located in the Worli district, this museum gives visitors an overview of Indian history dating back to pre-historic times.
- It is not a fancy place, by any stretch, but the basic information is key to understanding the background of this country and its people. –
- Admission is free, but if you don’t have a few hours to stand around and read the exhibits, you can spend $1.25 for a 90 minute audio tour (60 minutes is enough if you don’t dilly dally).
- _Bonus tip_: for less than $2, visit the Planetarium at the Nehru Center. –
- Read more about the Centre on [a previous post](https://www.earthvagabonds.com/dont-miss-nehru-centre-in-mumbai/).

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201000%20435'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 2\. Walk Juhu Beach

- Juhu Beach is one of the city’s most affluent areas. It’s roughly 15 kilometers north of Mumbai’s city center.
- Juhu Beach is a couple of kilometers from the western rail tracks and stations.
- This is a great walking beach because it’s mostly flat, sandy, and it’s more than five kilometers long, with a few vendor options (no beer).
- Locals do swim here, but water quality is questionable.
- _Bonus tip_: the International Hare Krishna Center is a short walk from the beach and offers a wonderful vegetarian lunch buffet for less than $7 at its restaurant, Govinda’s.

![juhu beach, mumbai, india](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20800%20600'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 3\. Walk Bandra’s Promenade (aka, Bandstand Promenade)

- This paved walkway along the rocky waterfront is only a kilometer long, and it’s also a popular spot with locals.
- Joggers Park is between two sections of waterfront walkways.
- The promenade ends at the Fort, which is next on the list.

![Ellen takes a photo on Bandra's Promenade.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20900%20506'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 4\. Visit Bandra’s Fort

- This old Portuguese place (built 1640) is a great spot to get a view of the Worli-Bandra Sea Link Bridge, with a partial Mumbai skyline. The best view is at the top of the Fort’s hill.
- Enjoy the park on the way down the back route – there are plenty of places to sit and catch a breeze with the local people.

![Skyline view of Mumbai from Bandra's Fort.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201000%20482'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 5\. “I Love Mumbai” sign

- There are more than one of these signs, but the one south of the Bandra highway gives you a view of the city across the water. It’s a bitch to find the park entrance – it’s sort of adjacent to a ramp onto the highway, and we saw no directional signs.
- Also, the park is closed from noon to 4:30 p.m., which we didn’t discover until we arrived.
- Note the maps so you don’t struggle like we did.

![theo and ellen in front of the "I love Mumbai" sign in Bandra.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20800%20600'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 6\. Gateway of India

- This giant archway was built for the British royals as a welcoming sign to India. It is a popular place for locals and tourists alike.
- Boats docked around the archway ferry people to other areas in the region, including the famous Elephanta Caves – a UNESCO World Heritage site. (But that trip isn’t free – it will cost about $10 for the ferry and the admission.)

![Gateway of India is a popular free thing to do in Mumbai.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20800%20600'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 7\. Taj Hotel

- This is a beautiful hotel near the Gateway of India and it’s another popular spot for tourists and locals. An oceanfront walkway crosses the front of the hotel where people line up for selfies.
- The hotel was one of the sites where terrorists attacked in 2008. Therefore, security in the area is tight, and if you wander into Starbucks for the clean facilities and an expensive cup of coffee ($9 (!) for one small and one medium latte), you will be searched and go through a metal detector.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20800%20600'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 8\. Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus (aka, CSMT)

- An impressive gothic-sytle building that is the headquarters of the Great Indian Peninsular Railway. Formerly named Victoria Terminus, it is an UNESCO World Heritage site.
- Local and some long-distance trains use this station.
- It’s especially gorgeous at night with the special lighting. There is a viewing platform across the street (it’s a wild intersection with many roads going this way and that).
- The best viewing, however, is on the street corner directly across from the station. Just mind the crazy traffic.
- _Bonus tip_: the bus station on the side has buses on main routes around Colaba.

![The famous CSMT train station in Mumbai.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20900%20506'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 9\. Hanging Gardens and Pramod Navalkar Viewing Gallery

- Fantastic oasis of nature in Mega-Mumbai. The Hanging Gardens draws out the local people for walks around the track when the sun is lower and it’s cooler.
- The viewing platform on the western edge of the gardens is three floors up. It showcases a spectacular view of a good part of the city, including Girgaon Chowpatty – an inner-city public beach.

![hanging garden, mumbai, india](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201000%20562'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

### 10\. The Gandhi Museum (my favorite free thing to do in Mumbai)

- Technically this is free, but a donation is much appreciated.
- [Mani Bhavan](https://gandhimuseum.org/site/gandian-institute/national/mani-bhavan/) is the house where Mahatma Gandhi stayed when he was in Mumbai.
- It’s stuffed with pictures and books and some of his most famous quotes. It also features items he used, such as spinning wheels to make cloth in the room where he stayed, shown in the photo below.

![Gandhi's museum is one of Ellens' favorite free things to do in Mumbai.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20900%20675'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Those are my **top 10 free things to do in Mumbai**, with some bonus tips for a little extra money. There are more free things to do in Mumbai, of course, such as temple visits and other areas to walk around the city.

Whatever you do and wherever you go, the people will greet you warmly and you will enjoy one of the most populated cities on Earth if you keep an open mind.

Sarvi Restaurant, situated in Byculla, is a renowned dining establishment that has been serving regional Indian cuisine and Chinese dishes for nearly a century. Despite its unassuming decor and no-frills service, the restaurant exudes an old-world charm that continues to attract crowds of patrons. The menu boasts classic chicken and mutton kebabs, rich Mughlai-style preparations, as well as more adventurous options like tongue masala fry and brain plain fry for those with an adventurous palate.

Slide 1 of 8

Sarvi Restaurant is an absolute delight for non-veg lovers! Their mutton and chicken seekh kebabs are unbelievably tender, juicy, and full of flavor — easily the highlight of the meal. The service is fast, and the taste is consistently excellent. Must-try items include the mutton seekh kebabs, chicken seekh kebabs, soft and fresh parathas, bheja masala fry, and their delicious kheema — every dish is rich, well-spiced, and satisfying. If you love authentic Mughlai and kebab dishes, Sarvi is a place you should not miss. Highly recommended!

Kyani & Co. is a historic Iranian cafe located in Marine Lines, Mumbai, established in the early 1900s and considered one of the city's oldest. It is popular among locals, especially college students and office workers who frequent the place for breakfast offerings such as sausages, fried eggs, bun maska, and Irani chai. The cafe also serves full meals like mutton dhansak, kheema pav, and chicken farcha later in the day.

Slide 1 of 8

Had the most amazing mutton puff, butter chicken puff, and mutton keema pav at this place. The puff was so buttery and flaky. The filling was tasty and sufficient. We had to take the ferry, otherwise we would surely have eaten more.
The management of this place should be a case study. Not fancy but so efficient. Understandable considering there’s always a huge line here. We went around 9:30 AM on a Sunday but didn’t have to wait more than 10 mins.
Make sure to carry cash as they don’t accept any other modes of payment.

I’d always wanted to visit one of the oldest bakeries in town ,Kyani & Co.and finally got the chance. The ambience is wonderfully nostalgic, filled with old-school charm, and I absolutely loved that part of the experience.

However, the food didn’t quite live up to the hype. The dishes we tried, like the kheema and bhurji, felt quite basic and nothing exceptional. On the brighter side, the snack items were much better , the mawa cake, chicken cutlet, and ,caramel custard were genuinely enjoyable.

Overall, the pricing is reasonable, making it worth a visit for the ambience and certain snacks, but don’t expect too much from the main dishes.

[Rebecca L — Google review](https://www.google.com/maps/reviews/data=!4m8!14m7!1m6!2m5!1sCi9DQUlRQUNvZENodHljRjlvT2t0clluWk5UME5yU21oRmFrNXVXRlpaYVZWcFJYYxAB!2m1!1s0x3be7ce6cde410629:0x1f92f4f701c5053d!3m1!1s2)

Kyani & Co. is a classic Iranian café serving authentic Iranian cuisine. The place is always crowded, and you’ll notice a good mix of locals and foreigners, which shows how popular and well-known it is.

Coming to the food, their chicken dishes stood out. The Chicken Cheese Kebab was actually very nice—it was stuffed with cheese from inside and had a hot-dog–like shape. It felt filling and had a good amount of chicken, which I liked the most.

I also tried the chicken samosa, but I felt the chicken quantity was a bit less, with more masala in the filling. Similarly, the mutton cutlet had more potato than mutton. Personally, I prefer meat-forward dishes.

The ambience is really great with an old-world charm, but photography is not allowed inside. I clicked one photo and was asked not to take pictures, which was a bit disappointing considering how beautiful the place is.

Overall, it’s an authentic Iranian café with a lovely atmosphere. The food is good, especially the chicken items, though the filling ratios may not suit everyone’s taste.

The unlimited thali meal includes a variety of traditional dishes such as dhoklas, bhajis, chutneys, rotis, puris, vegetable and pulse preparations, dal rice, khichdi and sweets. Slide 1 of 8

Shree Thaker Bhojnalaya – A Timeless Taste of Authentic Gujarati Thali

Shree Thaker Bhojnalaya is one of the most iconic and beloved places to experience authentic Gujarati cuisine. Known for its traditional thali, warm hospitality, and consistent quality, this legendary eatery has earned a special place in the hearts of locals as well as visitors. Dining here feels less like eating at a restaurant and more like being welcomed into a Gujarati household.

The moment you enter Shree Thaker Bhojnalaya, you are greeted with simplicity and warmth. The interiors are modest, clean, and functional, reflecting the traditional values of Gujarati culture where food quality and hospitality matter more than luxury décor. The seating arrangement is organized, and despite the heavy rush during peak hours, the staff manages the crowd efficiently.

The highlight, without any doubt, is the Gujarati Thali. The thali is a wholesome and balanced meal that represents the true essence of Gujarat’s culinary heritage. It usually includes a variety of rotating dishes such as shaak (vegetable curries), kadhi, dal, rotli or puri, rice, khichdi, farsan, chutneys, pickles, and traditional sweets like shrikhand or mohanthal. Each item is freshly prepared and served hot.

One of the most impressive aspects of Shree Thaker Bhojnalaya is the unlimited serving system. The staff continuously serves food with great attentiveness, ensuring that guests never feel rushed or restricted. The flavors are authentic—mildly spiced, well-balanced, and comforting—making the food suitable for all age groups. The use of fresh ingredients and traditional cooking methods is clearly reflected in the taste.

Historically, Shree Thaker Bhojnalaya has been serving Gujarati food for decades and is considered a cultural landmark. It has preserved the original style of Gujarati dining, where meals are meant to nourish both the body and the soul. Many regular visitors associate the place with nostalgia, family gatherings, and cultural pride.

Cleanliness and hygiene are well maintained throughout the restaurant. Plates, serving areas, and dining spaces are kept tidy, even during peak hours. The staff is polite, disciplined, and well trained, adding to the overall pleasant dining experience.

The pricing is reasonable, especially considering the quality, quantity, and authenticity of the food served. It offers excellent value for money and is often recommended as a must-visit place for anyone wanting to experience true Gujarati cuisine.

Shree Thaker Bhojnalaya attracts a diverse crowd—families, elderly guests, tourists, and food lovers from across India. Despite the popularity and long waiting times during weekends, the management ensures smooth operations and quick table turnover without compromising service quality.

Overall, Shree Thaker Bhojnalaya is not just a restaurant but a celebration of Gujarati tradition, flavors, and hospitality. If you want to experience a soulful Gujarati thali prepared with authenticity and served with warmth, this place is an absolute must-visit. It leaves you with a satisfied heart, a happy stomach, and a deep appreciation for Gujarat’s rich culinary culture.

That is an excellent request! Sardar Pav Bhaji in Tardeo, Mumbai, is an iconic institution, famous for its rich and buttery take on this quintessential Mumbai street food.
Here is a detailed review based on its reputation, customer feedback, and specialty:
🧈 Sardar Pav Bhaji (Tardeo, Mumbai): Detailed Review
Sardar Refreshments (popularly known as Sardar Pav Bhaji) has been serving its famous dish since 1966. It is located near the Tardeo Junction and is a pilgrimage site for pav bhaji lovers.
🌟 The Specialty: What Makes it Famous
The reputation of Sardar Pav Bhaji rests almost entirely on one factor: the butter.
\\* The Butter Factor: Sardar is legendary for using an extremely generous amount of Amul butter in their preparation. The bhaji (vegetable curry) is cooked with butter and then topped with a thick, visible slice or chunk of butter just before serving. This makes the dish incredibly rich, aromatic, and decadent.
\\* The Bhaji (Curry): Unlike many street versions that are bright red from artificial food colour, Sardar's bhaji is often noted for having a more natural, brownish/orange hue. It is made with fresh, mashed vegetables (potatoes, tomatoes, capsicum, peas) cooked slowly on a charcoal fire and features a unique blend of "secret masalas."
\\* Texture: The bhaji is well-mashed and has a perfect, thick consistency that is deeply flavourful beneath the butter.
\\* The Pav (Bread): The pav is equally important; it is generously butter-sautéed (often right on the tawa with the bhaji masalas) and served hot, making it soft, moist, and savory.
\\* Consistency and Legacy: The restaurant has maintained a long-standing reputation for using fresh vegetables and consistent flavor, which is a key part of its appeal and legacy.
🍽️ Food & Taste Profile
\| Feature \| Description \|
\|---\|---\|
\| Overall Taste \| Rich, savoury, buttery, and flavourful. It is typically less spicy than other street vendors but can be customized with their special garlic chutney. \|
\| Bhaji \| Creamy, well-mashed, and has a natural, non-artificial colour. The freshness of the vegetables is often noted. \|
\| Pav \| Soft, thoroughly buttered, and slightly crispy on the outside from being toasted on the tawa. \|
\| Menu Variety \| Highly focused. The main options are Amul Pav Bhaji, Cheese Pav Bhaji, Jain Pav Bhaji (no onion/garlic/potato), and Khada Bhaji Pav (unmashed vegetables). They also offer Masala Pav, juices, and cold beverages.
✅ Summary and Recommendation

Sardar Pav Bhaji is more than just a meal; it’s a Mumbai experience.
\\* Go if: You are a tourist, a die-hard pav bhaji enthusiast, or someone who believes "butter makes everything better." It is the ultimate indulgence for this dish.
\\* Be prepared for: A high price point, a heavy meal, and a wait time to get a table.
If you are craving the richest, butteriest, and most famous plate of pav bhaji in Mumbai, Sardar is the place to be.

Yazdani Restaurant & Bakery is a charming, old-school Iranian bakery and cafe located in Mumbai. Established in 1953, it has retained its nostalgic ambiance with vintage decor and handmade baked goods. The menu features a variety of Persian breads, delectable treats like Apple Cinnamon Pie and Carrot Cake, as well as the popular bun maska enjoyed with Irani chai. The rustic setting with old posters and advertisements on the walls adds to its retro charm.

Slide 1 of 8

Yazdani Bakery is one of those places in Mumbai that feels frozen in time. Started in 1953, it has been run by the same family for generations and still carries the old Irani café charm. The bakery is located in an old heritage building near Fort and Colaba, and the moment you step inside, you feel like you’ve walked into a different era — with its wooden furniture, old photographs, and simple, no-nonsense setup.
Yazdani is best known for its brun maska (soft bun with butter) and Irani chai, which is probably the most popular order here. Their mawa cake is legendary — rich, soft and full of flavour — and often sells out quickly. Other favourites include khari biscuits, apple pie, plum cake, and freshly baked breads and cookies. Everything tastes homemade and fresh, which is what keeps people coming back.
The place is not fancy, and service is simple, but that’s part of its charm. You come here not for luxury, but for nostalgia, honest food, and a slice of old Bombay. If you want to experience Mumbai’s Irani café culture and enjoy some classic bakery items, Yazdani is a must-visit.

Yazdani Bakery is more than just a place to grab a bite; it's a living monument to Mumbai’s Irani cafe heritage. Opting for a takeaway from this institution is a smart choice for those eager to savor its legendary bakes without the old-school dine-in experience (currently limited anyway).

While the interior retains a charmingly worn, antique aesthetic, the focus here is the edible legacy. The staff can occasionally be brisk, but the efficiency ensures a quick transaction. A Yazdani takeaway isn't just buying baked goods; it's securing a comforting, consistent piece of culinary history to enjoy in your own space. It's an indispensable, buttery, sweet slice of Mumbai.

The Legend of Ashok Vada Pav: Kirti College's Culinary Icon
Near the venerable Kirti College in Mumbai, a humble stall operates, not just selling food, but crafting a bona fide legend: Ashok Vada Pav. This isn't merely a snack; it's a rite of passage for students, a pilgrimage for foodies, and an emotional touchpoint for Mumbaikars.
The experience often begins with a legendary wait. Long queues, stretching like an academic semester, attest to its magnetic pull. But once you reach the counter, the reward is immediate. The vada itself is a masterpiece—crisp, perfectly fried, encasing a potato filling that is subtly spiced, favoring texture and freshness over overwhelming heat.
What truly elevates this vada pav is the signature accompaniment: the 'Choora Pav'. This unique addition, featuring the crunchy, spiced chura (fried gram flour remnants) mixed with the dry, potent chutneys, is stuffed generously inside the soft pav along with the vada. The resulting bite is a symphony of contrasting textures—soft, fluffy pav against the crispy vada and the granular, spicy crunch of the chura.
While some critics point to its smaller size or the premium pricing (a minor quibble for an institution), the enduring popularity is undeniable. Ashok Vada Pav manages to feel authentic and tapri (street stall) genuine, despite its enormous fame. It’s more than a quick bite; it's a flavorful slice of Mumbai's street food history, maintaining its crown through decades of consistent, unforgettable taste.service can be slow,,,

What once started as a humble snack joint has now expanded into multiple shops lining the streets of Colaba, proudly carrying forward the brand name and its historical recall. Unfortunately, nostalgia alone doesn’t translate into a good meal anymore.

I visited Bademiya purely for its legacy, but the experience was quite disappointing. The taste was nothing extraordinary, the service was painfully slow, and considering the portion sizes, the pricing felt unreasonably high.

Bagdadi Restaurant, located in Colaba, is a long-standing establishment that has been serving delicious Persian cuisine for over 125 years. Despite its simple decor, this non-vegetarian eatery is renowned for its flavorful Mughlai dishes and perfectly cooked tandoori specialties such as Shami kebabs and tangdi kebabs.

Slide 1 of 8

We visited Baghdadi Restaurant—an old-style gem! The food was absolutely tasty. The atmosphere was great, though it was quite crowded. We waited around 10 minutes for our turn—wait times vary with the crowd. We ordered Baghdadi Tandoori roti, chicken khara masala, and buff bhuna—all delicious! Plus, the prices were reasonable. Definitely worth a visit!

[Sohail S — Google review](https://www.google.com/maps/reviews/data=!4m8!14m7!1m6!2m5!1sCi9DQUlRQUNvZENodHljRjlvT2xKdVNIQkdlaloyZG0xSk4yMTNaMFZ6TjFKdFQwRRAB!2m1!1s0x3be7d1c13cf23657:0xc232a07282f7088a!3m1!1s2)

One of the legendary Halal restaurants in town, definitely value for money, but food-wise not that great.

The fried chicken is their most popular dish, but I felt it lacked salt. On the other hand, the Mutton Nihari is a must-try. We really enjoyed it. Coming from Kerala, where biryani is everything, I found their chicken biryani highly overrated and quite disappointing. (Maybe this is how Mumbaikars enjoy biryani, because the person who recommended this place loves it, but I felt the opposite.)

Overall, it’s a good place to visit and very pocket-friendly, but don’t expect outstanding taste in the food.

[Nihal M — Google review](https://www.google.com/maps/reviews/data=!4m8!14m7!1m6!2m5!1sCi9DQUlRQUNvZENodHljRjlvT2xkak0yZG1XVTh4ZGxWU1FUaEZiMHhmZUc4dGVWRRAB!2m1!1s0x3be7d1c13cf23657:0xc232a07282f7088a!3m1!1s2)

[Anish K — Google review](https://www.google.com/maps/reviews/data=!4m8!14m7!1m6!2m5!1sCi9DQUlRQUNvZENodHljRjlvT21nM09YVk9YMjlqWnpSYVR6bGhiRzVLTUc5UVIyYxAB!2m1!1s0x3be7d1c13cf23657:0xc232a07282f7088a!3m1!1s2)

Location & Popularity
Bagdadi is located in a prime area of Colaba, making it easily accessible and always buzzing with people. The restaurant is extremely popular, especially during evening hours, which clearly reflects its strong reputation among food lovers.

Waiting Time
Due to the heavy rush during peak hours, particularly in the evenings, customers usually have to wait for their turn. While the wait can be a bit long, it also speaks volumes about how loved the food here is.

Food Quality
The food at Bagdadi is genuinely great. The flavors are rich, consistent, and worth coming back for. It’s one of those places where the taste truly lives up to the hype.

Ambience & Renovation (Personal Opinion)
In my personal opinion, the restaurant could really benefit from a renovation. The place feels a bit dated, and a refresh would greatly enhance the dining experience without taking away from its old-school charm.

Final Verdict
Bagdadi is a must-visit for its excellent food and prime Colaba location. Despite the waiting time and the need for renovation, the taste and authenticity make it well worth the experience—especially for those who don’t mind a little wait for good food.

Highway Gomantak is a family-run seafood restaurant in Mumbai that offers a cozy and unpretentious dining experience. The restaurant is known for its authentic Goan cuisine, with over 30 varieties of thalis to choose from, including unique options like halwa curry thali and mori masala thali. The simple and hygienic ambience adds to the charm of this popular eatery located in Mumbai's bustling Gandhi Nagar region.

Slide 1 of 8

In a very long time, I wasn’t filled with such a subtle and home-blend restaurant. Calling it a restaurant might be over exaggerating because this place is run by a family and the authentic Goan food that they serve just makes you feel at home. This charming place is nestled right beside the highway, amidst a small colony of homes. It’s seamlessly blended in, creating an atmosphere that feels more like a family’s home than a resting place.
We have got the Surmai Fish Curry Thali and the classic Chicken Masala Thali. Both were just amazing and homely to taste.

Their staffs are very friendly and sweet enough that you feel like home.

While the quantity of food didn’t quite match the pricing, the quality was great.

This is very good place to recommend for a family lunch/dinner. I am sure you won’t be disappointed with it. Enjoy.

[Rebecca L — Google review](https://www.google.com/maps/reviews/data=!4m8!14m7!1m6!2m5!1sCi9DQUlRQUNvZENodHljRjlvT2podE0wYzJkVmhETUMxNVgzWmhVRUp3Y0cweWFIYxAB!2m1!1s0x3be7c921baaaaaab:0x6a1d06beadfb8656!3m1!1s2)

Extremely Disappointing & Overpriced – Not Worth It
This was one of the worst seafood dining experiences I’ve had in Mumbai.
I ordered a Pomfret thali and a Surmai thali. Instead of simply taking the order, the waiter confusingly asked whether I wanted a fish fry thali or fish curry thali. The menu clearly just mentioned “fish thali”—there was no categorisation, no explanation, nothing. All thalis were broadly priced around ₹350, so naturally we assumed standard thalis like any normal Malvani/Goan restaurant.
For context, I am from Malvan and have eaten seafood across Mumbai and coastal Maharashtra—this is the first time I’ve ever been asked something so vague without clarity on pricing.
When the Pomfret fry arrived, I was genuinely shocked:
No taste
No spice
No marination
Fish did not taste fresh, despite specifically confirming freshness while ordering
It felt bland, lifeless, and nowhere close to authentic coastal seafood.
I had clearly requested bhakri instead of chapati for one thali and vade for the other, yet the waiter didn’t bother noting it and served chapati. I had to ask for a replacement, which should never happen after a clear instruction.
We also ordered Bombil fry as a starter, which again was average at best and absolutely not worth the price.
Now comes the biggest shock.
Based on the menu, I was expecting a bill of around ₹1300. Instead, I was handed a bill of ₹2255.
Apparently:
Surmai “special” fish fry thali – ₹900
Pomfret thali – ₹650
Bombil fry – ₹450
Extra charges for bhakri
None of this pricing was ever explained while placing the order. We were never told that we were ordering a “special fish fry thali”. The Surmai fry was nowhere near worth ₹900—neither in taste, portion, nor quality.
When I raised this issue with the manager/cashier, his attitude was shockingly arrogant and disrespectful. No apology, no attempt to explain properly—just pure indifference, as if overcharging customers is normal practice.
To top it off, I overheard another lady nearby saying she had high expectations from this place and was equally disappointed.
Verdict:
Overpriced, tasteless food, misleading menu, careless service, and arrogant staff.
I would strongly NOT recommend Highway Gomantak to anyone—especially if you understand or appreciate real coastal seafood. There are far better, more honest places in Bandra and Dadar that respect both food and customers.

Prakash Shakahari Upahar Kendra in Dadar, Mumbai is a casual eatery known for its traditional Maharashtrian breakfast. The spot offers a variety of vegetarian dishes such as Batata Vada, Kanda Poha, Vada Pav, Sabudana Vada, and Sabudana Puri. The humongous Batata Vadas are particularly popular and the poha is made in the authentic Maharashtrian style.

Slide 1 of 8

Visited Prakash Shakahari Upahar Kendra, Dadar West and had an amazing experience! Tried their Dahi Misal, Aloo Vada, and Kharvas for dessert. The Misal was perfectly balanced — not too spicy, which really allowed the rich flavor of the spices and farsan to stand out. The Batata Vada was tasty and fresh, and the Kharvas was super soft with a smooth texture. Overall, the food quality and traditional flavors were excellent. Just a note — they don’t accept online payments, so make sure to carry some cash when you visit. Highly recommended!

Prakash Shakahari Upahar Kendra is an iconic spot in Dadar with a rich legacy of over 50 years. It’s a wonderful place to experience authentic Maharashtrian cuisine.

Don’t miss their legendary drink, Piyush—it’s even available in a half portion, so you can enjoy it without getting too full from just one item. Their thalipeeth is truly next level, and the sabudana vada served with a unique groundnut chutney is absolutely delicious.

The place does not offer any parking.

A must-visit point of interest when you’re in Dadar.

Prakash Shakahari Upahar is a familiar old-school spot in Dadar, popular for traditional Maharashtrian breakfast items. My experience was mixed and mostly average.
I tried the Thalipith, which was genuinely good in taste and felt fresh—easily the best item I had. The misal was average and surprisingly mild, lacking the expected spice punch. The tea was honestly quite bad, with poor taste and no real depth.
One thoughtful and uncommon decision is that they don’t serve pav at all. While many may not like this, I actually appreciated the intent—it feels health-conscious and shows they’re thinking beyond pure business.

Cafe Mondegar, located in Mumbai, is a legendary spot that offers a vibrant nightlife experience. It was the first restaurant in the city to feature a jukebox and is adorned with captivating murals depicting life in Mumbai and the cafe's atmosphere. The menu boasts delicious offerings such as cheese grilled sandwiches, chaat, pasta, and paneer tikka along with an impressive selection of beers.

Slide 1 of 8

Visited Cafe Mondegar on a Saturday, the wait time was 20 minutes, which is pretty normal for this place. The vibe is very much that of a busy bar with great music, lively energy, and a crowd that adds to the experience.

The service was excellent, our server Nirmal was amazing, extremely welcoming, and the food arrived quickly despite how packed it was. That really stood out.

We tried Fish Fingers and Chips, Chicken Spring Rolls, Chicken Arabiata, Chicken Burgers, French Fries, Chicken Reshmi Tikka, Caramel Custard, and Chocolate Mousse.

Everything was a 10/10 in terms of taste and quality, except the fish fingers, which can be skipped.

I visited Cafe Mondegar for the very first time during my trip to the Gateway of India. Frankly, its popularity is what pushed me to try it, but after visiting, I couldn’t really understand what all the fuss is about.

It’s a very average café with a room packed so tightly that even mosquitoes might struggle to find space to breathe. The tables are placed extremely close to each other, making it uncomfortable to move around. That said, considering the heavy crowd and waiting time to get a table, the service was commendable — our order arrived within 10 minutes.

For food, we ordered a Corn & Cheese Pizza, Cheesy Garlic Bread, and fresh Wheat Beer. The pizza was loaded with cheese, but it wasn’t properly melted — more stiff than the satisfying cheesy pull you’d expect. The garlic bread, however, was soft, crunchy, and definitely better than the pizza. The wheat beer was fresh and enjoyable.

Overall, my experience remained average, mainly due to the long wait, overcrowded seating, and the constant pressure to vacate the table quickly for the next guests and also the prices for such an experience are sky high.

For me, this was surely a first and last visit.

A perennial favorite among locals and tourists alike, Haji Ali Juice Centre is an iconic culinary landmark nestled at the threshold of the historic Haji Ali Dargah. Since its inception in the 1960s, this bustling establishment has cultivated a legendary status, evolving from a modest stop for pilgrims into a vibrant gastronomic institution. It is celebrated for its unwavering commitment to quality, utilizing fresh, seasonal ingredients to craft an extensive repertoire of refreshments that have become synonymous with Mumbai's street food culture.
Reviewers frequently highlight the establishment's ability to maintain high standards of hygiene and flavor despite the immense daily crowds. The atmosphere is quintessentially Mumbai—a high-energy, casual setting where patrons often enjoy their treats standing on the pavement or from the comfort of their cars, adding a unique drive-in charm to the experience.
• Signature Fruit Creams: The "Sitaphal" (custard apple) cream is universally acclaimed as a must-try masterpiece, featuring a luscious, thick consistency generously laden with fresh fruit chunks.
• Exotic Shakes & Juices: Guests often praise the Mango Milkshake for its rich, creamy texture and the "Triveni"—a sophisticated blend of mango, strawberry, and kiwi juices.
• Savoury Accompaniments: Beyond beverages, the menu boasts popular fusion snacks like the Jain Pizza and the indulgent Cheese Toast, noted for its generous cheese-to-bread ratio.
• Late-Night Accessibility: Operating from the early morning until well past midnight, it serves as a reliable sanctuary for night revelers seeking high-quality refreshments.

Kala Ghoda Cafe is a modern and artistically minded cafe and gallery located in the Kala Ghoda area of Mumbai. It offers a variety of gourmet Western-style breakfasts, as well as tea, coffee, and juice. The cafe is popular among locals and artists, with limited seating available. One of its popular offerings is the dark chocolate waffle. For those looking for healthier options, they also serve Desi waffles made from gluten and wheat-free batter sourced from Uttarakhand.

Slide 1 of 8

Visited Kala Ghoda Cafe during the Kala Ghoda Festival with friends, and what a find this place turned out to be. Tucked away inside a small lane, it’s a little difficult to spot. After the madness of the fest, this café felt like a lake in a desert, felt calm, comforting, and exactly what we needed.
The vibe is warm and lively at the same time, with a charming setup and even a hidden bar counter that adds to the character of the place.
Coming to the food and drinks, they are the absolute winners. I tried the Masala Cappuccino, and it was truly unique, with a lovely kick of masala chai flavours blended into the coffee. Something I’ve never had before and surprisingly addictive.
The Cheese Chilli Toast, recommended by the waiter, did not disappoint—super cheesy with perfectly crispy bread. The Cottage Cheese Burger was honestly to die for, easily one of the best vegetarian burgers I’ve had—flavourful, filling, and perfectly balanced.
And the real star of the show was the Hash Brown dish “Rosti, crispy on the outside, creamy on the inside, and just cooked to perfection. Absolute comfort food.
Overall, great food, lovely coffee, welcoming vibes, and a peaceful break from the festival rush. Kala Ghoda Cafe is definitely a place I’d keep coming back to.

Pancham Puriwala is a historic Indian cafe that has been serving delicious snacks and traditional plates for over 150 years. Founded by Pancham Sharma, the eatery has expanded over seven generations and continues to attract eager clientele with its mouthwatering delicacies such as khichdi, crispy bhindi curry, potato curry, and various types of puris.

Slide 1 of 8

Located within walking distance from CSMT railway station, Pancham Puriwala is a convenient stop for a quick meal. I visited on a weekday evening and it wasn’t much crowded. The ambience is simple and average, but the food stands out—fresh, tasty, and true to its legacy. The staff was polite and courteous, making the experience pleasant.
Knowing its rich history dating back to 1848 adds an extra charm to the visit. A great spot for a satisfying North Indian meal.

Cafe Irani Chai in Mahim scores high on location and accessibility. It’s conveniently situated with easy access from Mahim railway station, and the connecting road makes local transport readily available—definitely a plus for first-time visitors or those exploring the area.

As a visitor, I was keen to try this place given its popularity and the buzz around its Irani-style offerings. The preparation style is indeed quite unique and different from what we usually get in the Delhi NCR region, which adds to the curiosity and appeal. However, when it comes to taste, nothing really stood out as mind-blowing.

The place is famous for its concept and the uniqueness of dishes on offer, but the flavours and aroma didn’t quite live up to the hype. I tried a fairly wide spread—Bun Maska, Mutton Keema, Irani Deluxe Chicken Cheese Burger, Veg Cheese Burger, and Paneer Bhurji. Among all of these, the Chicken Cheese Burger was the most flavourful and enjoyable. The rest of the dishes, unfortunately, felt quite average.

One thing to note is that all dishes—whether gravy-based or dry—are served with pav (if needed). You won’t find rotis or parathas here, which aligns with the Irani café concept.

Overall, Cafe Irani Chai is worth a one-time visit if you’re keen on trying something that’s quite famous and culturally distinct. But from a taste perspective, it didn’t leave a lasting impression and isn’t something i would consider a go-to place.

A friend's scouring of places and suggestions bought us to the Good Luck Restaurant, in Bandra. It is situated right next to Mehboob Studio, at a busy junction in Bandra. The place is more known for it's breakfast dishes, and is usually crowded.

The ambience is vintage, takes you back to the old Bombay nostalgia, and the menu is typically Parsi. They have a small convenience store as well.

The food is a mix of typical Bombay Parsi and middle eastern. We were pretty hungry, and started off with a bunch of pavs and kheema fry beef. Served piping hot, the crunchy pavs go wonderfully well with the spicy beef kheema. Next we ordered, the kheema ghotala beef, which had more of an egg consistency. I personally liked the kheema fry more than the kheema ghotala. Next up was the lovely chicken shawarma, with generous amounts of chicken and mayo.

The flagship dish of this place is the bun maska accompanied by Irani chai which soon followed suit. A few mutton samosas later, we ordered the final dish of the day - more crunchy pavs with Chicken Handi, upon the recommendation of the waiter. It was a tad bit disappointing compared to the earlier dishes.

Overall, the food gets a healthy rating of 4/5, the vintage ambience another 4/5. Service was pretty fast as we were one of only 3 tables at 8PM on a Friday evening. A great visit if you're in the area, and are looking for a filling meal at a reasonable price.

Waah apruh Taj !!!

The Taj Hotel took about 14 years to build and was opened for guest in 1903. The foundation was laid by Jamshedji Tata. In the year 1889, founder of Tata Group Jamshedji Tata (Jamsetji Tata) suddenly announced that he is going to build a grand hotel in Bombay (now Mumbai)

When Jamshedji Tata announced to build Taj Hotel Mumbai, his family burst out. Tata's sisters started protesting to him. Author Harish Bhat writes in his book 'Tata Stories' published by Penguin (Hind Pocket Books) that a sister of Jamshedji Tata said in Gujarati, 'You are building a science institute in Bangalore, setting up an iron factory and now you are building a hotel in Bombay?”

Harish Bhat writes that Jamshedji Tata's mind had not only come to the idea of building a grand hotel in Bombay, but there was a story and fire of revenge behind it. In those days, the Watson’s Hotel used to be the most famous Watson’s Hotel in the Black Horse area of Bombay, but only Europeans got access. Once Jamshedji Tata reached there, he did not get entry due to not being European. This hurt his self respect.

Besides those days there was no hotel in Bombay that could compete with Europe or Western countries. Jamshedji Tata often visited America, Europe and Western countries and saw hotels and other amenities there, Harish Bhat writes. An article published in 'Saturday Review' in 1865, which questioned when will Bombay get a good hotel to suit his name? This write up touched Tata's heart.

Jamshedji Tata, went to every corner of the world to buy stuff for Taj Hotel. Markets from London to Berlin were searched. The Taj Hotel was India's first hotel where carbon dioxide ice construction plant was installed to keep the rooms cool. The lift for the hotel was ordered from Germany and the fans came from America. The pillars came from Paris to put in the Hall's ballroom.

Those days, the total cost of Taj hotel had reached 26 lakh rupees. Finally when the Taj hotel was opened in 1903, its room rent was kept at Rs. 6 per day. It was almost equal to contemporary hotels. But only 17 guests reached the hotel on the first day. The situation has been almost the same for the next few days. Taj hotel expenses created an economic crisis in front of Jamshedji. Some people started saying this even Jamshedji's "white elephant".

Elco is a Mumbai-based fast food joint that specializes in chaat items. Their most popular dish is pani puri, which is made right on the spot. They also have a variety of other snacks, including pav bhaji and idli sambhar. The restaurant was clean and the bathrooms were very clean. Overall, this place is definitely worth checking out if you're looking for some delicious chaat dishes!

Slide 1 of 8

We started with the Mutton Dum Ki Rani, which was exceptionally flavorful—rich, aromatic, and cooked to perfection. The Masala Kulcha complemented it beautifully, being soft, fresh, and perfectly balanced in taste. This combination was easily one of the highlights of the meal.

The Chelo Kebab truly stood out as one of their authentic signature dishes. The kebabs were juicy, perfectly seasoned, and packed with flavor, reflecting the restaurant’s legacy and expertise. A must-try for anyone visiting Peter Cat.

The Grilled Chicken with sauce (sizzler) was well-prepared and tasted good overall. It was served on a sizzling platter with an appealing presentation, adding a premium and visually impressive touch.

For dessert, we chose the Brownie with Vanilla Ice Cream and Hot Chocolate. The flavors were rich and indulgent; however, the brownie felt slightly overcooked at the bottom and had become a bit hard. Aside from this minor detail, the dessert was enjoyable.

The ambience is classic and elegant, with a timeless, old-world charm that truly defines the place. The warm lighting, comfortable seating, and calm atmosphere create a refined and pleasant dining environment.

Overall, an impressive experience with high-quality food, excellent presentation, and a sophisticated ambience. Highly recommended.

The restaurant has a clean and casual ambiance, making it perfect for families, friends, and even solo diners. Babu Vada pav is essentially a takeaway snack joint on the street; they have been operating in that location for decades. They transformed from a street food vendor on a wheeled cart to a takeaway snack joint.

There is no seating available so basically you can order a TAKEAWAY or have it on a disposable plate.

It's one of the "go-to" places for snacks in a 10 kilometre radius; Quality & is taste is a function of who's making the vada pav batter or batata bhaji ; salt / green chilli/ garlic proportions vary from time to time.

Likewise perception of service can also vary depending on who's on the service side of the counter or the type of crowd at peak hours

In addition to their Vada Pav, Patti Samosa and Kothimbir Vadi are also to be savoured once. Sabudana vada is also good going by reviews of many esteemed local guides

The type of snacks served uses copious amounts of garlic without which vada cannot get its taste; so if you are finicky about not having garlic for whatever reasons you may have to think twice before consuming

One of their dry chutneys also contains dry coconut and peanut in addition to garlic ; if you have allergies be aware of them before consuming

Parking is available on alternate sides of the streets on odd days and even days , but the proximity to street corners and bus stops make it a challenging task ; during off peak hours parking is available but the snacks may not be piping hot at that time.

There is also a school nearby so it can be chaotic during school rush hours or in the evening between 1730 - 1930 due to peak station going traffic

They do not sell any beverages but there is a sugarcane juice stall, tea stall nearby and several stores where one can buy bottled water or cold beverages.

Summarily definitely a decent place to have a small snack and if you are a regular you'd know when to visit them
